steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting GNNUERS, a framework that explains user unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems with counterfactual reasoning. Cover the motivation, the research gap, how the approach works at a high level, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: explaining unfairness in recommendation
- Counterfactual explanations for GNNs and the research gap
- Our approach: GNNUERS
- Use of ground truth labels and global explanations
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - recommender systems more effective/sophisticated; complexity raises worrying questions
  - properties beyond effectiveness: trustworthiness, fairness, explainability
  - usually treated independently, one at a time
  - fairness (main case study): equitable recs for users + providers, but service providers (e.g. online platform) need to know why the model is unfair
  - fairness in an explainable way = central yet under-explored
  - few existing approaches use user/item features to characterize disparities
  - explanations limited to those features; features hard to obtain, most models use user-item interaction data
- Counterfactual explanations for GNNs and the research gap
  - XAI: techniques to find relevant data entities as explanations
  - counterfactual methods recently effective for explaining GNN predictions
  - GNNs effective on graph data: information retrieval, recommender systems, NLP, user profiling
  - counterfactual reasoning also used to guarantee fairness in GNNs by manipulating topology, various downstream tasks
  - no approach yet to explain unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems
  - not a simple application: original methods on classic graphs, recommenders are bipartite (users and items)
  - -> efficiency issues, detailed in Section 4
- Our approach: GNNUERS
  - GNNUERS = GNN-based Unfairness Explainer in Recommender Systems; shift of paradigm
  - perturbs original bipartite graph to find user-item interactions leading to user unfairness
  - removing selected edges -> fairer recommendations; global explanation of when model generates disparities
  - guided by demographic parity: all demographic groups get same recommendation utility (utility = usefulness for (a group of) users)
  - perturbation driven by counterfactual reasoning: assume a set of edges missing
  - counterfactual world (no interaction) vs actual world (edges present)
  - loss: i) minimize utility disparity across groups, ii) minimize number of perturbed edges
  - interactions cherry-picked so model on graph without them gives fairer recs at inference
- Use of ground truth labels and global explanations
  - loss has access to ground truth labels of the evaluation subset
  - -> monitor recommendation utility on evaluation set for all demographic groups
  - crucial to select interactions causing utility disparity
  - distinguishes GNNUERS from recent procedures that modify recs to mitigate unfairness; we explain it instead
  - model-level (global) explanations for system designers and service providers
  - experiments in Section 5: systematically explains user unfairness, uncovers patterns
- Contributions
  - from research gaps (Section 2): formulate problem of explaining unfairness in GNN-based recommenders (Section 3)
  - framework for global counterfactual explanations of unfairness (Section 4)
  - validation: three state-of-the-art models, four data sets, key utility metrics (Section 5)
  - implications for future research (Section 6)

Novel recommender systems are more and more effective and sophisticated, and they excel at satisfying users’ preferences. But the way these systems function has also become much more complex, and this raises worrying questions. On top of this, there is the prominent importance of preserving properties that go beyond recommendation effectiveness, like trustworthiness, fairness, and explainability. However, the modern literature usually treats all these issues as independent perspectives and mostly tackles them one at a time. Take algorithmic fairness as an example (it is also the main case study of our work): it is extremely important to give end users and content providers equitable recommendations, but it is also important for service providers (e.g., an online platform) to understand why the model behind their platform is unfair. So tackling algorithmic fairness in an explainable way is a central but under-explored area. The few approaches that exist for explaining unfairness in recommendation use user and item features to characterize the disparities a model generates. Their methods do uncover the features related to the model disparities, but the explanations they generate are limited to those selected features. And these features might be hard to obtain, because most recommendation models work with user-item interaction data.

If we look at other areas of explainable artificial intelligence, various techniques have been used to find the relevant data entities that can serve as explanations for different tasks. Recently, counterfactual methods have become an effective way of explaining the predictions of models based on Graph neural networks (GNNs). steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Novel recommender systems are more and more effective and sophisticated, and they excel at satisfying users’ preferences. But the way these systems function has also become much more complex, and this raises worrying questions. On top of this, there is the prominent importance of preserving properties that go beyond recommendation effectiveness, like trustworthiness, fairness, and explainability. However, the modern literature usually treats all these issues as independent perspectives and mostly tackles them one at a time. Take algorithmic fairness as an example (it is also the main case study of our work): it is extremely important to give end users and content providers equitable recommendations, but it is also important for service providers (e.g., an online platform) to understand why the model behind their platform is unfair. So tackling algorithmic fairness in an explainable way is a central but under-explored area. The few approaches that exist for explaining unfairness in recommendation use user and item features to characterize the disparities a model generates. Their methods do uncover the features related to the model disparities, but the explanations they generate are limited to those selected features. And these features might be hard to obtain, because most recommendation models work with user-item interaction data.

If we look at other areas of explainable artificial intelligence, various techniques have been used to find the relevant data entities that can serve as explanations for different tasks. Recently, counterfactual methods have become an effective way of explaining the predictions of models based on Graph neural networks (GNNs). GNNs have proven effective at modeling graph data in several domains, for example information retrieval, recommender systems, natural language processing and user profiling. Approaches based on counterfactual reasoning have also been used to guarantee algorithmic fairness in GNN-based models, by manipulating the topological structure for various downstream tasks. However, as far as we know, nobody has proposed an approach to explain unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems. Filling this gap is more than just applying counterfactual explanation methods for GNNs to uncover unfairness in recommender systems. The original methods for explaining predictions in GNN-based models are applied to classic graphs, while recommender systems are bipartite, since they connect the interactions between two types of entities (nodes), i.e., users and items. This causes efficiency issues, which we go into in detail in Section 4.

In this work we propose a shift of paradigm. We present a framework called GNNUERS (GNN-based Unfairness Explainer in Recommender Systems), which perturbs the original bipartite graph to identify a set of user-item interactions that lead to user unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems. With our approach, user unfairness can be uncovered by the selected edges, i.e. the user-item interactions. Removing them from the original graph can give fairer recommendations for the end users, and so it globally explains under which conditions a model generates disparities. Concretely, our approach is guided by the demographic parity principle, which makes sure that all demographic groups get the same recommendation utility, where the utility of a recommendation is how useful it is for (a group of) users. Under this paradigm we propose a perturbation mechanism that is driven by counterfactual reasoning. The goal is to change the users’ recommendation by assuming that a set of edges is missing from the graph. In other words, we modify the original bipartite graph assuming that certain users have not interacted with the items of the selected edges (in the counterfactual world), while in reality the graph does include these edges (in the actual world). The user-item interactions are selected using a loss function with two terms: i) minimizing the disparity in recommendation utility across demographic groups, and ii) minimizing the number of perturbed edges. The user-item interactions are cherry-picked so that a model using a graph without them can generate fairer recommendations during the inference phase.

Note that the loss function that guides the perturbation mechanism has access to the ground truth labels of the subset of data used for evaluation. This means our approach can monitor the recommendation utility measured on the evaluation set for all the demographic groups. This is crucial for selecting the specific user-item interactions that lead to the utility disparity across demographic groups in the recommendations of GNN-based systems. Because it uses the ground truth labels of the evaluation subset, GNNUERS is different from other procedures recently proposed in the recommendation literature. Those procedures try to modify the recommendations to mitigate the unfairness issue, while our method focuses on explaining it. So GNNUERS can generate explanations of user unfairness at the model level, also called global explanations, which can give system designers and service providers insights on how to improve the fairness of the model. The experiments in Section 5 support this claim, and show that our framework can systematically explain user unfairness and also uncover existing patterns that justify why unfairness was characterized.

Our contributions are the following:

- • Starting from the research gaps in the current literature (Section 2), we formulate the problem of explaining unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems (Section 3) and we propose a framework that generates global counterfactual explanations of unfairness (Section 4);

- • We validate our proposal on three state-of-the-art models with four data sets, measuring key utility metrics (Section 5), and finally we discuss what our work implies for future advances in this research area (Section 6).

In this work, we propose a shift of paradigm by presenting a framework, named GNNUERS (GNN-based Unfairness Explainer in Recommender Systems), which perturbs the original bipartite graph in order to identify a set of user-item interactions leading to user unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems. With our approach, user unfairness can be uncovered by the selected edges, i.e. the user-item interactions, whose removal from the original graph can result in fairer recommendations for the end users, thus globally explaining under which conditions a model generates disparities. Concretely, our approach is guided by the demographic parity principle, which ensures that all demographic groups receive the same recommendation utility, where the utility of a recommendation denotes its usefulness for (a group of) users. Under this paradigm, we propose a perturbation mechanism driven by counterfactual reasoning, whose goal is to alter the users’ recommendation by assuming that a set of edges is missing from the graph. In other words, the original bipartite graph is modified under the assumption that certain users have not interacted with the items of the selected edges (in the counterfactual world), while in reality the graph includes such edges (in the actual world). The selection of user-item interactions is driven by a loss function combining two terms: i) minimizing the disparity in recommendation utility across demographic groups, and ii) minimizing the number of perturbed edges. Specifically, the user-item interactions are cherry-picked such that a model using a graph without them generates fairer recommendations during the inference phase.

It should be noted that the loss function guiding the perturbation mechanism has access to the ground truth labels of the subset of data used for evaluation. Our approach is therefore able to monitor the recommendation utility measured on the evaluation set for all demographic groups, which is crucial to select the specific user-item interactions that lead to utility disparity across demographic groups in the recommendations of GNN-based systems. By leveraging the ground truth labels of the evaluation subset, GNNUERS distinguishes itself from other recently proposed procedures in the recommendation literature: while these aim at modifying the recommendations to mitigate unfairness, our method focuses on explaining it. Therefore, GNNUERS can generate explanations of user unfairness at the model level, also denoted as global explanations, that can give system designers and service providers insights on how to improve model fairness. This claim is supported by the experiments in Section 5, which show that our framework systematically explains user unfairness and also uncovers existing patterns that justify why unfairness was characterized.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • Based on the research gaps in the current literature (Section 2), we formulate the problem of explaining unfairness in GNN-based recommender systems (Section 3) and propose a framework to generate global counterfactual explanations of unfairness (Section 4);

- • We validate our proposal on three state-of-the-art models under four data sets, measuring key utility metrics (Section 5), and finally discuss the implications of our work for future advances in this research area (Section 6).
